explain.say: The Moon goes round Earth about once a month, passing between us and the Sun at every new moon. So why isn't there a solar eclipse every month?

explain.say: The Moon's orbit is tilted by about 5 degrees compared with Earth's path round the Sun. Most months the Moon slips just above or below the line to the Sun, and its shadow misses Earth.

faq.q: Why don't we get an eclipse every month?
faq.a: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit. At most new and full moons, the Moon passes a little above or below the line between Sun and Earth, so no shadow lands where it would make an eclipse.
asks: Why isn't every new moon an eclipse?

faq.a: It is a window of about five weeks, roughly every six months, when the Sun lies near one of the two points where the Moon's orbit crosses Earth's. Any new or full moon then can produce an eclipse.

faq.q: How many eclipses happen in a year?
faq.a: Every year has between four and seven eclipses, solar and lunar together, and always at least two solar eclipses, though many are only partial.
Eclipses repeat in a pattern every 18 years and about 11 days, called the saros. Ancient Babylonian astronomers used such patterns, and today computers work out eclipse paths centuries ahead.

faq.q: Why do solar and lunar eclipses come in pairs?
faq.a: In an eclipse season the Sun, Earth and Moon stay nearly lined up for weeks. A new moon then gives a solar eclipse, and the full moon two weeks before or after can give a lunar one.
asks: Do eclipses come two weeks apart?

facts: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5.1 degrees to the plane of Earth's orbit.
There are between four and seven eclipses every year, counting solar and lunar.
The saros cycle of about 18 years 11 days was used by Babylonian astronomers to predict eclipses.
